## Website Designer in Pune: What Figma's 2026 AI Agent and Code Layers Change About the Design Handoff

Figma's 2026 Config conference introduced an AI agent that works directly inside the design file, plus a feature called Code Layers that lets working code sit alongside static design elements on the same canvas — and together they're changing the handoff between a website designer in Pune and the developer who builds what they've designed, not by removing either role, but by moving the line between them. The old handoff — a designer exports a finished mockup, a developer interprets it and writes code from scratch — is being replaced in parts of the industry by a workflow where design and code exist closer together from the start. Whether that's a genuine improvement or an added layer of tooling complexity depends heavily on how a design team actually uses it, which is exactly the question worth asking before you brief your next project.

If you're planning a new website or a redesign, you don't need to become an expert in Figma's release notes. But you do need enough of a working understanding to ask your designer a few pointed questions, because "we use the latest AI tools" is a marketing line, and "here's specifically what changes for your project's timeline and cost" is the answer that actually matters to you.

## What Actually Launched in 2026

**A canvas-aware AI agent.** Beginning in a beta rollout from May 2026, Figma introduced an AI agent that understands the design canvas directly — not a general-purpose chatbot bolted onto the interface, but a system that can read the actual layers, components, and structure of a specific design file and act on it. It can be given "skills," which package a team's specific conventions and workflows into reusable instructions, and "connectors," which let it reach other tools a team already uses — project management boards, documentation systems, code repositories — and push updates back into them.

**Code Layers.** Announced at Config 2026, this feature lets a developer place executable code directly onto the design canvas as a layer, sitting alongside the more traditional static design elements. The stated goal is closing the gap between "this is what the design should look like" and "this is the code that produces it," so the two aren't maintained as entirely separate artefacts that drift apart over a project's life.

**Design System Intelligence.** A set of tools aimed specifically at the problem of design systems decaying over time — components getting used inconsistently, tokens (the underlying values for colour, spacing, and type that a design system is built from) falling out of sync between the design file and the actual production code. These tools flag inconsistencies and suggest fixes rather than requiring a manual audit each time a design system starts to drift.

**AI-assisted image editing built into the canvas.** Background removal, object isolation, image expansion, and basic enhancement are now available without leaving Figma for a separate tool like Photoshop, which mostly matters for speed during the exploration phase of a project rather than changing what a finished website ultimately looks like.

## What This Actually Changes for a Client Briefing a Website

### Faster early exploration, not faster final judgment

The AI agent and image tools genuinely speed up the early, messy part of a design process — trying five different layout directions, generating placeholder content, testing a colour direction against real proportions instead of an abstract swatch. What they don't do is replace the judgment call about which of those five directions actually serves your business and your customers. A designer using these tools well should be moving through exploration faster and spending the time saved on getting your specific brief right, not skipping the thinking part of the process entirely and handing you AI output with a coat of polish on top.

If a designer's pitch is essentially "the AI will figure out what works for your brand," that's a warning sign regardless of how impressive the AI's output looks in a demo. The tools are good at generating plausible options quickly. They have no actual knowledge of your customers, your competitors, or what's worked and failed for your business specifically — that context still has to come from a human designer who did the work of understanding your brief.

### A tighter, faster path from design to working code

Code Layers matters most for projects where design and development have historically drifted apart — a designer ships a beautiful mockup, a developer builds something close but not identical to it because translating every detail by hand introduces small deviations, and by the third design iteration nobody's entirely sure whether the "source of truth" is the design file or the live site. For a website designer in Pune working closely with an in-house or partnered development team, tools that keep design and code more tightly linked can shorten this drift meaningfully, provided the team actually uses the workflow as intended rather than treating it as an optional extra nobody gets around to setting up properly.

For you as the client, the practical benefit is fewer "that's not quite what we agreed on" moments during development, because the handoff has less room for interpretation error between what was designed and what gets built.

### Design systems that stay consistent for longer

If you're commissioning a site with more than a handful of page templates — a multi-location business, an e-commerce catalogue, an NGO with several programme pages — a design system (a defined, reusable set of components, colours, and type rules) is what keeps every new page looking like it belongs to the same site rather than a patchwork built by different people at different times. Design System Intelligence tools that catch drift automatically are useful specifically because that drift is otherwise slow and easy to miss — nobody notices that a button style has quietly forked into three slightly different versions across a site until someone happens to look at them side by side.

## What to Ask a Website Designer in Pune About Their Tooling

- **"Are you using AI tools to speed up early concepts, or to generate the final design I'll sign off on?"** The honest answer should be the former. A designer who's applied judgment to AI-assisted output is doing something meaningfully different from one who's forwarding it with minimal changes.
- **"How closely does your design file match what the developer actually builds, and what's your process for keeping them in sync?"** This question matters regardless of whether they use Code Layers specifically — it's really asking whether design and development are coordinated or working from separate, drifting versions of the truth.
- **"If my site has multiple page types, do you build and maintain an actual design system, or design each page individually?"** Individually designed pages tend to look fine at launch and grow inconsistent within a year as new pages get added by whoever's available at the time.
- **"What happens to the design files after handoff — do I own them, and can a different developer pick up the project later if needed?"** This is a business continuity question independent of any specific tool, and it's worth asking on every project regardless of what design software is used.

## A Worked Example of Where the Difference Shows Up

Consider two website designer briefs for the same kind of project — a mid-sized e-commerce store with roughly thirty product category pages that all need to look consistent.

In the older, disconnected workflow, a designer creates one polished template in a design file, a developer builds it, and then as the catalogue grows, new category pages get added by whoever's available — sometimes a developer eyeballing the original design, sometimes a template edited without the original designer's involvement. Six months later, the sale badge is a slightly different colour on category pages added in month four versus month one, nobody remembers deciding that, and fixing it means auditing every page manually.

In a workflow that uses a properly maintained design system with drift-detection built in, that inconsistency gets flagged early — the design tooling notices a component has diverged from its defined standard and surfaces it, rather than requiring someone to spot it by eye across thirty pages. The AI tooling here isn't doing the design work; it's doing the tedious consistency-checking work that a human would otherwise have to remember to do manually and reliably won't, especially months after launch when attention has moved on to other priorities.

## Why This Matters More for the Devices Most Visitors in India Actually Use

A design that looks polished on a large desktop monitor during a client presentation doesn't automatically translate into a good experience on the mid-range Android phone and average mobile data connection that a large share of Indian website visitors actually use. This isn't a new problem introduced by AI design tools, but it's worth raising here because faster exploration can tempt a team to skip the slower, less glamorous step of testing designs specifically on realistic devices and connections rather than the designer's own high-end laptop and office Wi-Fi.

Design System Intelligence and drift-detection tools help keep a component library consistent, but they don't by themselves verify that a heavy hero image, an animated interaction, or a large embedded video actually performs acceptably once real-world network conditions are factored in. That verification step — testing on a genuinely average device, on a throttled connection, not just checking that the design looks right in a browser preview — is still a manual discipline a design and development team has to build into their process deliberately. Ask directly whether your website designer in Pune tests on real mid-range devices as a standard step, not an occasional one reserved for when something's already gone wrong after launch.

## How to Evaluate a Portfolio for These Specific Skills

A portfolio full of polished final screenshots tells you very little about how a designer actually works, because a finished screenshot looks similar whether it took a disciplined, well-tested process to get there or a rushed one. A few more useful questions to ask when reviewing past work:

- **"Can you show me a project where the design and the live site match closely, and one where they drifted — and why?"** A designer who can answer this honestly, including admitting where something didn't go as planned, is more trustworthy than one who claims every project went perfectly.
- **"Do you have an example of a multi-page project where the design system held up well after new pages were added later?"** This tests exactly the consistency-over-time problem discussed above, rather than a single polished landing page.
- **"What does your design-to-development handoff document actually look like?"** Whether or not a designer uses Code Layers specifically, there should be some concrete artefact — specifications, a shared component library, documented spacing and type rules — that a developer can work from without guessing.

## What Hasn't Changed, and Won't

**Understanding your business is still entirely a human job.** No AI tool, however capable, has visited your store, spoken with your customers, or sat through a meeting where you explained why your previous website underperformed. That context is the actual input a good design brief runs on, and it comes from a conversation with a designer, not from a prompt.

**Accessibility and usability testing still need a human eye and, ideally, real users.** AI-assisted design tools can flag some technical accessibility issues — contrast ratios, missing alt text patterns — but whether a checkout flow is genuinely easy to use for a first-time visitor on a mid-range Android phone with an average mobile connection is a judgment call that needs real testing, not an automated check.

**A cheaper price for "AI-assisted" work isn't automatically a worse or better deal — it depends entirely on what happened to the time saved.** If a designer is charging less because they're spending less total time on your project, ask directly what got cut. If they're charging the same but redirecting the saved exploration time into more rounds of refinement and testing on your specific brief, that's a genuine improvement in what you're getting for the same money.

### Does using AI design tools mean a website designer in Pune should charge less?

Not necessarily, and it's worth being specific about why. If AI tools speed up early exploration and that saved time gets reinvested into more careful refinement, testing, and attention to your specific brief, you're arguably getting more value for the same price, not less. A lower price only makes sense if the designer is doing less total work on your project as a result, which is a different question worth asking directly rather than assuming from the tooling alone.

### Will my website end up looking generic if it's designed with AI-assisted tools?

That risk is real, but it comes from how the tools are used, not from the tools existing. A generic-looking website is usually the result of a designer accepting AI-generated output with minimal customisation for your specific brand and audience. The same tools used by a designer who applies real judgment to your specific brief, tests options against your actual customers rather than generic assumptions, and pushes back on AI suggestions that don't fit your brand will not produce a generic result — the differentiator is the human decision-making layered on top, not the tool underneath it.

### Do I need to understand Figma or any specific design tool to brief a project properly?

No. What you need to communicate is your business goals, your audience, examples of things you like and dislike, and any specific functional requirements — the tool your designer uses to translate that into a working website is their responsibility, not something you need to evaluate directly beyond asking the questions covered above.

### Is Code Layers something only large agencies can realistically use?

It's a genuinely useful workflow for any team where design and development are coordinated closely, regardless of size — the constraint is whether the team has set up the workflow properly and trained everyone involved to use it consistently, not the size of the studio. A small, well-coordinated team can use it effectively; a larger team that hasn't actually adopted the workflow properly gets none of the benefit despite having access to the tool.

## How This Fits Into Your Design Brief

If you're planning a new site or a redesign, our guide on [what to expect from a professional website design process](/blog/website-designer-pune-guide-2026) covers the fuller brief beyond tooling specifics — timeline, revision rounds, and what a proper design process should include. And if performance and accessibility are a specific priority for your build, our piece on [Core Web Vitals and accessibility](/blog/website-accessibility-core-web-vitals-designer-pune-2026) goes deeper into how those get measured and tested independently of design tooling.

## How We Approach This at Govindani Infotech

Our design team uses modern tooling to move faster through early concept exploration, but every design that reaches a client for sign-off has had a human designer's judgment applied to it specifically for that business — we don't forward AI-generated concepts without that layer of review. On projects with multiple page templates, we build and document an actual design system from the start, specifically so consistency doesn't quietly erode as new pages get added months after launch by whoever happens to be available. Our [website design and development](/services/website-creation) team treats the design-to-code handoff as something to plan for explicitly, not something that's assumed to just work out.

If you're briefing a redesign and want a process that moves quickly where speed doesn't cost you quality, and stays careful where it matters, get in touch through our [contact page](/contact-us) to talk through your specific project.
